utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to update you on the situation with respect to the matters we discussed at the end of last week relating to the remaining witnesses for -- for the Lukic Defence team. The one individual, Mr. Kovacevic, who we had had at the end of the week did have to go back to Belgrade to urgently attend to the matter that we discussed -- that we discussed in private session. He left yesterday. We're hoping still to get him back. In the meantime the statements for the person that we've proposed as 6D-2, although as I understand it there's not yet a decision on those protective measures, so that's why I was saying the man we've proposed as 6D-2, his statement was made available -- the translated version and the B/C/S version were made available on Saturday -- Saturday -- Sunday -- pardon me, Sunday morning, whereas Mr. Zlatkovic's was just made available late last night, I would say even early today since I doubt anyone was on their e-mail except for myself at midnight. We have gone through this weekend and tried to contact the remaining witnesses and see who is available and what the prospects are for the rest of the case, and the way we see it we would be able to -- we would be able to present 6D-2 tomorrow, that would give everyone the 48 hours' notice. If parties waive 24 hours of Zlatkovic's notice, we could also do Mr. Zlatkovic tomorrow and finish both tomorrow. Otherwise, the alternative would be to have Mr. Zlatkovic on Wednesday. We would be prepared to present the expert Mr. Simonovic also on Wednesday, I don't know how long he would take, but we would have approximately I think two to three hours in direct. Zlatkovic would only have 30 minutes to 40 minutes in direct. 6D-2 as I see would have very little in direct. 6D-2 would have 10 to 15 minutes or so, even under half an hour. Then we would have still in play we have the individual that we have proposed as 6D -- the individual that we have proposed as 6D-1 for which Your Honours might recall the -- there was a matter from last week about that witnesses's ability to attend. I believe the last communications we had with that individual are that if protective measures are granted she -- they would be able to attend and we would have, as I said, Mr. Kovacevic hopefully returning and one other witness for whom I think that that witness would -- has a protective measures request being made. But in any event even if we look at the worst-case scenario and have our next witness called on Wednesday, which I think is even more than worst-case scenario, we would still complete our remaining witnesses by the beginning of next week, which I think in the overall picture is -- is the best we can do under the circumstances, and that involves of course the decisions we made this weekend after contacting witnesses to trim down our list quite significantly and also provide everyone a fair opportunity to have the statements with enough time to -- to -- to cross -- to prepare for cross-examination on them. I believe 6D -- the person disclosed as 6D-1 and the last person whose name I'm not going to say in open court because I believe that there's a protective measures motion being prepared as we speak, those two would be live witnesses, but they would not -- I think 6D -- 6D-1 would probably be an hour and a half -- so we would probably do -- probably try to do a short statement with that individual and have one and a half hours maybe of direct if -- if that much, and then with the last individual they would be very -- I think -- they would probably be live because I don't think we would have time to prepare that one, but I would not anticipate more than an hour and a half, two hours for that one as well. Long and short of it, Your Honours, we don't have a witness that we can -- well, we do have 6D-2 here, but as I understand it from talking to colleagues that they would be objecting -- strictly adhering to the 48 hours' rule on the statement and again we have very limited direct for the individual, but 6D-2 is -- and of course there is the issue of the protective measures not yet being ruled upon. So we're at Your Honour's mercy basically for how to proceed, but again we re-assure that if our proposals are acceptable to the Court we will of course endeavour and I think we will successfully complete our witnesses by the beginning of next week, well before the scheduled break in the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're having some difficulty making clear to us the position in relation to protected and potential protected witnesses, so we shall briefly go into private session so that we can unravel your tongue on that; but I do understand your difficulty.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis, is there to be a response in relation to 6D-2 and the protective measures for that witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour, we are going to request that we have at a minimum the 48 hours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. 6D-2 protective measures, can we deal with that. We are awaiting your response and I think today may be the 14th day for the response on that witness, and that's the only reason no decision has yet been taken on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I guess I wasn't aware of that. I was thinking of 6D-1, we had filed our response --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We dealt with that, but there is another one and that relates to the witness proposed as 6D-2. The measures sought I think are voice and image distortion and pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We certainly don't have an objection to the pseudonym, Your Honour, and off the top of my head I don't have an objection to the face and voice distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ivetic, you -- your application for the pseudonym for that witness and the use of image distortion and voice distortion is granted. We note that there's no opposition from the Prosecution, but in any event the application is justified and the usual conditions that apply, the other ancillary conditions will apply to that. Now ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That then disposes of that aspect of that witness's evidence, and we can now turn back to the witness for whom the pseudonym 6D-1 --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, there may be confusion on my part, but if we could stick with 6D-2 for a moment, I'm being told that the application did ask for closed session for that witness as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a second. That's not my understanding, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm told that the -- although the witness notification -- the partly confidential part of the witness notification said pseudonym and voice distortion, that the actual application from the 20 -- 31st of March did ask for closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I have your application here, Mr. Ivetic, and there is no request for closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then there must be some -- I'm told paragraph 9(b) made reference to it, that's what the e-mail from back in the office is directing to, but in any event I do know from meeting with the witness with my colleague Mr. Lukic that the witness had been insistent that -- that they were concerned that without closed session, their identity could be made known by the circumstances of their --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there's absolutely nothing about that in this application. That was the position in relation to 6D-1.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct, 6D-1 we're clear on. It's 6D-2 that we ought to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You had such a narrative in the--

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- application for 6D-1. But there's no such narrative in this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that might cause a problem for us, because as I indicated I believe the witness in question was rather -- rather firm on -- on that request of us. So it may have been -- it may have been an issue where we in filing did not include all the necessary -- one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, when we have a break you can review the situation. The application that has been made has been granted; it can be varied if that can be justified, but that's a matter for you. Now we can return to the situation of witness 6D-1. I think we made it clear when dealing with that matter last week that if the issue of protective measures did arise we would review the position. So that what you're asking us to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour, based upon our information that should be -- that issue should be reviewed so that we can make plans to try and have the witness attend here under the conditions that were sought if the Court is willing to grant the conditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis, do you have anything more to say on that one?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if the witness attends here we were willing to agree that her testimony be taken in private session, and we can address after her testimony if there's some parts that should be made public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In the case of the witness for whom the pseudonym 6D-1 is proposed, we are satisfied that voice and image distortion alone would not be sufficient to protect the identity of the witness so if -- so we would grant the application for the pseudonym and evidence in private session -- in fact, in closed session, closed session, and that again will be subject to the usual conditions that accompany such decisions. That then takes us to the issue of how we are to address the evidence of the witness Radovan Zlatkovic. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, this was a witness that was originally listed as being a witness that would testify last week. Near the end of the week we raised the issue that we had not yet received a statement for him, that we had some concerns about what we saw as a vagueness item in the 65 ter notice. We did eventually receive some clarification on that, but we did not receive his statement until I think about 11.43 p.m. last night. Ms. Kravetz is the lawyer who is intending to cross-examine that witness and she didn't see it until she same in this morning. So we would stand by the 48-hour notice and ask that he not take the stand until at least late yesterday -- Ms. Kravetz tells me she could be prepared to cross-examine him tomorrow, I think I said late yesterday, I meant late tomorrow. We could do that but we are not prepared to cross-examine him today and we don't think we should be required to. We had some indication I thought on Friday from the Defence counsel that they expected to receive his statement that day. I think this was the one they indicated they'd farmed out to Belgrade, and for some reason we did not get it until a quarter to midnight last night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One other way of dealing with the witness of course, is not to have the statement but to hear the witness today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That is a possibility, Your Honour, I know we've we done that sometimes in the past, but because we expect a statement our preparation sort of is on hold until we see the statement and then we decide what documents we need, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The issue in this situation is what is in the interests of justice, because it's only -- if it is in the interests of justice that a statement is admitted. Now, that's the foundation for your objection to proceeding with the statement straight away today because the interests of justice demand that you have more time to prepare cross-examination. You'll naturally get that when you hear the evidence viva voce because it takes longer and you are able to take it in and assess the questions to ask as it goes along. It would assist us to know by which means you prefer to proceed, in particular are you content that it's by statement because at least you know where you stand on that or do you take a different position in light of our willingness to consider other options?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May I have a moment to consult?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Or maybe I can address that, Your Honour. We have no preferences. If Defence wants to lead the witness live, that's not a problem. What I would request is a bit more time to conduct my cross-examination later because they've just notified a new video which I haven't seen and since I just got the statement I may have additional exhibits that I want to add to my list that are not there, so that's the only thing I would request. But if my colleagues want to lead him live, that's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you're okay with tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, I'm okay with tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And who's dealing with 6D-2, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what's your position on that one?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I received his statement I think yesterday -- well, it was sent yesterday at 10.00 in the morning. We would request that we not start cross-examination of him until tomorrow as well. The statement I think is 34 pages long. I heard I think this morning that direct examination would be fairly short, but I'm giving you notice now that I may request longer than an hour to do cross-examination depending on what's in the statement. There are some five pages of exhibits listed for him, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic, there is the option of proceeding with one or other of these witnesses live.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The problem being that both witnesses have very extensive written statements and to do viva voce would be spending just as much time. We still at the end of day be here as long as we are, just with a lot more court time and a lot more difficulties, especially dealing with introduction of exhibits, since the statements do try to introduce exhibits in them so as to speed up the process and make it more manageable for everyone. We would prefer I think the -- our position would be that we intend to present these witnesses as 92 -- part of their testimony pursuant to 92 ter and part live as we've indicated and that would be our position on the matter given -- as I said, this -- the witness, Zlatkovic, we cut down his statement in order to get the translation done in time to, I believe, 18 pages and so I still have to prepare to try and get the -- that's why -- that's why there would be half an hour to 40 minutes for that witness in live to try and highlight some of the points in the material that I had to cut out of the statement in order to get the translation done in time because, again, we had the difficulties with the translation. Our preference and our stand would be to present them both via live/92 ter, and that would, I think, if counsel from the other side are saying that they would be able to do Zlatkovic in the afternoon tomorrow we would be able to present him tomorrow and we could perhaps even finish both witnesses tomorrow. It would again depend on the extent of the cross-examination of the other parties and the Prosecution, which I don't know the extent of, but in any event we would still be on track then to complete the expert and the remaining witnesses that we have -- that we now have in play --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think we're talking about the afternoon. We're talking about tomorrow, full stop. Is that correct, Ms. Kravetz?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, that's no problem if it's morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I take it you have no problem with actually hearing such direct as there is of Zlatkovic this morning and then adjourning the cross-examination until tomorrow .

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, I understood that was the question Your Honour was putting to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There isn't a problem, Mr. Ivetic, about leading your witness in one form or another today, the problem relates to the cross-examination. So we will certainly be hearing Zlatkovic's evidence in chief this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It might take longer since I had the -- I have only half the questions prepared for -- with the material without --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry ?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The issue is we had to take out a lot of material from the statement to get the translation in time to even get it to get it to the parties s last night. So I still have a set of I think it's ten pages of the -- of the original statement that I have to look through and try and pull out questions from so I would be hard-pressed to confine him within half an hour and get it all done efficiently and with the interests of my clients.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You have the luxury of being able to take your time. There wouldn't also be a problem by giving you an hour to prepare yourself to do that. We obviously have time and we should use the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could get two hours to do that, then I'd be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You were obviously a negotiator in another life.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm just trying to be balancing the interests of all the parties and especially my client who I have to keep in mind and knowing the material I have and the state that I'm in, I think that I would need at least two hours to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay, the final piece in this jigsaw to enable us to prepare things would be any assistance that we can be given in relation to the time that will be occupied by Simonovic. How long is your chief likely to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Between two and three hours would be the direct for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Who's dealing with that witness. Mr. -- Mr. Stamp, how long do you envisage in cross-examination for him?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't think it would take more than two sessions, three to four hours, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Two sessions for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that indicates that we really need -- if we're going to finish his evidence as well as the other evidence this week we really need to have started his evidence on Thursday at some stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I think we indicated that we would -- we should be able to finish -- we should be able to start him on Wednesday I think based upon our estimate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I doubt it in light of what Mr. Hannis has said about cross-examination of 6D-2. So I think being more realistic you're talking about Thursday for Simonovic. Now, we don't have Mr. Visnjic with us. His deputy on expert witnesses is who?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Five days' notice for experts is what we were told on Friday. There is a possibility now of expert evidence next week. So that should be taken into account, and you can start making arrangements now. I think we would be assisted -- sorry, Mr. Hannis, do you want to intervene on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Maybe you were about to speak what I had a question about. There was also the additional witnesses the Ojdanic team had requested and got permission for regarding the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, I had forgotten that. So it looks like evidence next week under your control in some way -- so -- Mr. Sepenuk, so we'll adjourn shortly, obviously to give Mr. Ivetic time to organize himself, and perhaps in that time you would consider the order in which evidence beyond the Lukic Defence case might be presented and what evidence it might be appropriate to bring next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The -- you mentioned last week that experts probably would not be called until after the break. I think you said that specifically, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah -- and not so long ago I said I thought they would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you see how things change.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No, I understand that, but we somewhat relied on the specific statement that you made. Now, I heard from the rest of my colleagues yet because there are other expert witnesses. Quite frankly, Your Honour, before you made that statement I was ready to bring one of our joint experts, that's Dr. Fruits and then after you made your statement I said well, that's probably the end of it. Now there are other experts, the handwriting folks, Mr. Fila has an expert, and Mr. Zecevic has an expert. So I think what we'd like to do is during this next hour or two - I understand that we're going to adjourn now - let's -- we'll talk about it and come back with some sort of a proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, I think somehow or other it's essential to have some of that evidence here next week in light of what's just been said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, I just wish to inform the Chamber that we all received Zlatkovic's statement last night. I haven't seen it yet nor have I had a chance to consult, so I won't be ready for the cross-examination before tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. If that remains the position we'll obviously have regard to it, but you will have some time now to have a look at it and see to what extent it affects you. I'm not so sure it does have a great impact on your case in any event. Now, Mr. Ivetic, it would be convenient if we resumed at 11.15, say, and we had an hour and a half during which we could probably be brought up-to-date on experts and hear your evidence in chief. Does that sound -- we can make it 11.30, if you feel you need the two hours, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, 11.30 would be essential so that we can perhaps even call back to the office and find out what the status of the last individual is as well so we can have a clear picture of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And if we did sit then, we -- the maximum -- well, we can sit for an hour and a three-quarters, which would take us to 1.15, if that would give us a reasonable prospect of doing all we can do today. If it's necessary to sit in the afternoon, then we would probably break at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fine. I'll try and confine my ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As I said, I should be able to confine my direct to the -- to well within the hour and hour and three-quarters that had been mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We shall adjourn now and resume at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The first -- before -- no, before the witness comes in -- just, sorry -- can we deal with the issues that were left outstanding or is time still required to deal with these? Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think that Mr. Visnjic would like to address this matter. You're talking about the experts now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, I think Mr. Visnjic would like to speak to this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as you are aware, I said on Friday that we need five working days. Unfortunately on the transcript on -- it says five days only, but it's five working days. But we will do our best to bring those witnesses. As things stand now, two witnesses will not be able to come next week, they're not available. We are gathering documents for the visas for two persons, and for the other two we will be in touch with the Victims and Witnesses Section to see whether they will be able to ensure air tickets for them on time. As for the timetable of testimony for next week, I suggest that we inform you about that a little later because we are -- still don't know exactly when the witnesses will be arriving in The Hague. Quite certainly they will not be available for next week, that is Stankovic and Lukic will not be available next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, there are two separate situations here. There's the evidence of Aleksic and one other witness in relation to handwriting. Perhaps you could give some thought to whether that might be dealt with next week. If that were the case, there would be no question of any more than one expert coming here just in case the time was available to deal with that expert. Should it not be possible to arrange the evidence of Aleksic and the other, then we would not expect more than -- we would not expect you to arrange for the attendance of more than two of the experts and possibly one would be more realistic. I think the best situation would be if we could deal with the handwriting and one of the experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, among the four people that are able to come, they may be able to come next week, Aleksic and a witness has been included and we are -- we have in mind only two more additional experts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you manage to get Aleksic and the other handwriting-related witness, if you manage to do that then I don't think it would be sensible to have more than one other expert here. So if that helps you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I can say is that the only question mark I have for the moment is Aleksic. As for the other witness, for the handwriting he will be available, of course on condition that the necessary visa arrangements are made so that now it is only Aleksic that is in question. So we would have Aleksic, the witness, and one expert. In that case we need to consult with Mr. Zecevic, too, because I think the joint expert that he will be leading is free only next week. So then perhaps he could be the expert witness. But this is still open until I know what the final situation is with respect to Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The one you're referring to is Jokic, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, that would be -- the ideal arrangement would be to deal with the two witnesses relating to handwriting and one expert, and we'll leave it to you to try to arrange that. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I may just interrupt shortly, Your Honours. I have made the arrangements already with Mr. Jokic to be present here on Wednesday -- I mean to give evidence on Wednesday, next Wednesday. The problem with Professor Jokic is that he can come in April but the problem would be for him to come in May because of some private and business obligations. Thank you very much. And I would like the Trial Chamber to consider that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So we'll leave matters there on the issue of the attendance of witnesses, and we will now proceed with the evidence of Mr. Zlatkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Wait, wait, hold on. Yes, Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: In the interim, Your Honour, as -- expecting that the witness wasn't going to come until after the break, I made some very mad phone calls in the interim period because, as I say, I was planning to have Dr. Fruits here before the break until Your Honour made that statement. So I think I'm prepared now to bring Dr. Fruits here next week; on the other hand, I don't want to -- if Your Honour has it in mind the two handwriting folks and the expert witness, other than Mr. Fruits -- Dr. Fruits, I can leave it at that, but I don't see any problem with having Dr. Fruits here also next week. But again, that's obviously -- I leave that to Your Honours' discretion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if it's fairly easy to make that arrangement, then it would be beneficial to have the option there. But bear in mind there are only four days available to us next week. And I think they are not days -- they are four-hour days as well. So you might -- we might manage him but it's not looking terribly likely, and that means him coming back at another stage. I take it he would go home again and come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yeah, right -- no, if he came, obviously, Your Honour, we would want to have him here and have him finish. He would be a maximum of I'd say less than an hour and a half, probably less than that and with the appropriate time for cross-examination. But I simply wanted to mention that to you because we have now made arrangements for him to come. But again, I leave it to Your Honours' discretion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, we will do our best to accommodate that arrangement, and obviously if Mr. Ivetic finishes on Monday and the handwriting were dealt with on Tuesday, there would be time on Wednesday and Thursday to deal with Jokic and Fruits. So it is a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So I'm grateful to you for that. Anyone else? All right. We can now continue with the evidence of Mr. Zlatkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zlatkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry you've been kept waiting so long there, but there have been procedural difficulties this morning. We've now resolved these as far as we can resolve them and we can proceed with your evidence. Would you, therefore, please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please don't apologise, there's no problem. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You will now be examined by Mr. Ivetic on behalf of Mr. Lukic. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Zlatkovic.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zlatkovic, in preparation for your testimony did you give a written statement to the members of the Sreten Lukic Defence team?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At this time with the usher's assistance I have a hard copy of 6D1627 in the Serbian language to give to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, while we're waiting for that, the rest of us can follow on e-court. If you could just look through this document and tell us, do you recognise this to be the written statement that you gave to the members of the Lukic Defence team for this case?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you have any corrections to make to this written statement?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: At the present, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, today you are under oath. If we asked you to testify on the same matters as set forth in the statement, would your answers be the same as those set forth therein?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would move to admit the written statement which is 6D1627 into evidence at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zlatkovic, apart -- or I should say I would like to first ask you to expand on a few matters from your statement, and first I would direct your attention to paragraph number 17 of the same, it's page 8 of the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I apologise, Your Honours, the English I don't seem to have in front of me. I guess the translation hasn't made it into my hands yet, but it should be about thereabouts on the English as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zlatkovic, you at paragraph 17 describe the shooting death of policeman Rajkovic Petar. Did you, in fact, form an investigation with respect to this incident, and did you ever as a result of your investigation determine from where he had been shot; and if so, upon what was this conclusion based?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 1998 I was asked to carry out an on-site investigation on the occasion of the death of Petar Rajkovic from the village of Dubac near Kovin because Rajkovic at the time was on the main road between Djakovica and Decani, a check-point in the village of Prilep, and he was hit from a mosque by sniper fire, that is, a projectile fired by a sniper. When I arrived on the spot I tried to carry out the investigation, but the commander of that unit was there, Stanimir Djukic, and I was unable to approach the location because I was prevented by sniper fire coming from the minaret of the mosque which was on the actual road in Prilep, when you're moving from Djakovica towards Decani this was on the right-hand side about a hundred or 150 metres along that road. So I was unable to carry out the on-site investigation. Later on the policemen -- actually, we tried two or three times, even using an armoured vehicle, but we could see the sniper fire coming from the minaret and we just couldn't reach there. The policeman was hit in the forehead.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I think that's -- we do have details of that in your statement. If we can now also then move to paragraph 30 of your statement, and therein you describe that already on the 25th of March, 1999, some parts of Djakovica were struck by the NATO air-strikes. And first of all I would ask you if you could give us some more details about some of the areas, particularly if any of them were civilian, that NATO bombed within Djakovica during this time-period.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: With the beginning of the NATO air-strikes, parts of the town of Djakovica were exposed, that is Cabran hill overlooking a part of the town -- Cabrat, and the whole centre of the town. As soon as the bombing started, I think it was on the 24th that it started. On the 25th a Tomahawk missed the target at Cabrat and fell in the central part of the town near -- next to the river, the very centre of the inhabited area where a number of shops were burned down as a result, the shops being made of planks. This whole street had wooden buildings along the sides and several Albanian homes were burned down as well, as the area was mostly inhabited by Albanians. This was close to the Hotel Pastrik.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look at Exhibit 6D538, and I believe, sir, that this is a criminal report or criminal denunciation relating to the event you just described. If you can look at pages 19 and 20 of the same there are some pictures, and I would ask you if these pictures comport to your recollection of the scene, that is to say if they are showing this area that you have told us about. And actually, I would --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: I see the report but not the photographs. Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: That is the street where these wooden huts were with shops and people mostly engaged in commerce.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And -- all right. Here and also I think in paragraph 33 you talk about fires arising from the NATO bombings. Could you tell us what was the capacity of the fire-fighting services within Djakovica to deal with these consequences of the NATO bombings? What was the fire-fighting capacity like?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: The fire-fighting units at the very beginning of the air-strikes and even before had strict orders coming from their own administration in Belgrade that as soon as anyone reports a fire of any kind, even of haystacks, that they should immediately extinguish those fires. They did that whenever they could when they were not prevented from doing so by terrorist attacks, or if it was not possible to extinguish the fires because of NATO bombs. Even in this particular instance they did go there and they took part in clearing away the rubble from the streets so as to make it open to traffic. But the fire-fighting unit in Djakovica I think had two motor vehicles so that at times it could not act in two or three places at the same time. They would go to extinguish one fire and then they would have to refill the water, but they did go out whenever that was possible and I saw them doing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can just briefly look at 6D30. In your statement you talk about how the situation of the NATO bombings was -- benefitted the activities of terrorists and criminals especially with respect to making the situation more untenable in Djakovica. If you could look at this crime report or criminal denunciation, I believe this is regarding the attack upon some members of the criminalistics police in Djakovica in park in front of the Hotel Pastrik. Do you recall this particular incident and does it reflect some of the -- do you recall more details of it and does it reflect some of the factors that affected the ability of the police to go out onto the scene within the city and do its work in terms of crime scene -- in terms of on-site investigations?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: This is a criminal report, and the damaged party is inspector Nenad Danilovic, who is from Pec. He worked in the SUP of Djakovica. His duties were to prevent general crime. Immediately after the raid he was in the park, in front of the Pastrik hotel, and he was hit there probably by a sniper because the bullet found in his arm by the doctor was established to have been fired by a sniper rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And if we can look at 6D489, and as we wait for this document I believe this is a criminal denunciation which you yourself prepared. If you could please confirm that for us and then give us any additional information or commentary that you can about this particular exhibit.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: In this case is something I testified about in this honourable Tribunal in The Hague in the case against Ramush Haradinaj in July, and I can say that in the course of 1998 we found out that close to the Radonjic lake and in the lake itself there was certain corpses, and I think it was towards the end of the month of August, the beginning of September that we somehow managed to get there and indeed we were able to see for ourselves that there were a number of bodies. In the lake itself we found two or three bodies and around the lake there were corpses which were in a state of advanced decomposition. Some of those bodies were identified, they were mostly -- or there were Serbs and Montenegrins and Romanis, and I think quite a number of Albanians too I'm afraid. And we found out through operative work that these Albanians were killed because they refused to subordinate themselves to the liberation army of Kosovo, that is, the terrorists who were led by Ramush Haradinaj and his men. A certain Rexha from Djakovica was killed only because he had the photograph of Slobodan Milosevic on one side and Shote Galica on the other, and it was for this reason that he was abducted between Suva Reka and Prizren, taken to the Radonjic lake, and executed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can move along, I think that that's covered and I think we've had other testimony about the investigations performed there. If we can take a moment to look at -- first of all, if you could look at paragraph 32 of your statement, and there you mention two incidents of ambushes in the region of Djakovica known as Cabrat. And for the first you give a detailed description of how the members of the police were injured, but for the second one you don't give as many details. Did you -- could you describe for us your knowledge of the ambush site for this second attack, that is, the 9th of May wherein Tomovic Stanko and some members of the VJ were subjected to -- subject to an attack by the terrorists.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. When the NATO forces arrived on the territory of the then-Yugoslavia, the terrorists entered Djakovica. They had already been in Djakovica but not in such large numbers. On that night - and this is just my operative information - a large group entered under the leadership of Arben Shkupi, a certain man called Lekaj and Aljbin Docaj. They immobilised the inhabitants of Djakovica, young people, and on the 7th of May there was a mixed patrol of the MUP and the VJ --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We have that, we have that in -- I'm talking about the second, about the second incident on the 9/5/1999, the 9th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The second half of that paragraph, the last -- the last sentence in Serbian or the last portion in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: What page?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 32 of the [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's all right. I found it. The terrorists in the Cabrat neighbourhood, which is underneath a peak, a mountain peak, and it's exclusively inhabited by Albanians, a mixed patrol set out to carry out its usual tasks, its regular tasks. Tomovic Stanko, a member of the police, was shot at from an ambush and he was hit in the back of his head and killed. On this occasion Aleksandar Rakovic, a sergeant, was killed. I knew this young man, he lived with his grandparents, he was an orphan, Milanovic Dejan, Ljubomir Miric and Srdjan Krstic, and Ivica Mitrovic were seriously wounded in that terrorist attack. The attack was totally unprovoked, they were simply on patrol, but they were ambushed and attacked by terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you describe from where the terrorists attacked these individuals, what -- from what structures they attacked?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: The terrorists in this particular instance attacked from an attic, and they had special loop-holes. Albanian houses have high walls around them, and they pushed out some of the bricks facing the street so that they could peer through those gaps and shoot from there. In addition to this, the terrorists had something they called "kapadjiki" [phoen] in that area. They could go from one yard to another, from one house to another. So while the police were shooting at one house they would already be in the second or third house in that row, firing from there. This was a perfidious method of fighting. In some cases Albanian civilians would be ploughing a field next to the road, and when a police patrol or a VJ patrol came along, he would fire at them and flee to the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in the course of performing your duties in Djakovica during the time-period of the NATO bombings, did you have occasion to perform on-site investigations for any NATO attacks in which civilians were -- in which significant civilian casualties were experienced?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the Maja settlement which is between Djakovica and the village of Bistrazin on the main road leading from Djakovica to Prizren on the left-hand side. There were some refugees living there from Croatia and Serbian Krajina, some 50 or so people. A man from the Serb Krajina who had fled before an attack of the Croatian forces had brought his horses there and was engaged in a transport business in Djakovica. That night the village was attacked and quite a few people were killed and many were injured. Inter alia, Darko Ulatovic [phoen] was killed, he was a retarded young man, and a waitress called Goca was killed and her child and her -- her daughter, that is. And there were quite a few people who were wounded. We managed to get some of them to hospital in Djakovica, and from there the most seriously injured were somehow transferred to the hospital in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you mentioned the number of people involved that were casualties of this NATO strike. What was the immediate effect of this event upon the civilians in Djakovica as you experienced?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: You mean in the Maja neighbourhood? Well, people were upset, Serbs, Albanians, Roma, and Egyptians, they were all uneasy and none of them believed they would not be bombed or killed by anyone so they all started moving out. Serbs, Albanians, Roma, Egyptians, they were all trying to leave, go to safety, and they were also afraid of the fighting between the KLA and the police and the army because the KLA was entering that area from every side and the area was no longer safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to -- or did you have occasion to perform any on-site investigations of any major incidents of civilian casualties from NATO on any of the roadways surrounding Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. This was in the village of Maja, and on the Djakovica-Prizren road near the Bistrazinski bridge when the NATO planes bombed two columns, two convoys, one which was on the way back from Prizren towards Meja and another which had set out towards the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What were -- how would you describe the efforts of the MUP of the SUP Djakovica in regards to this investigation -- this on-site investigation and with regards to the victims of the same?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: We were informed that this incident had taken place in that area and we set out with several teams. We even asked for an ambulance from the hospital in Djakovica and a vehicle that had been mobilised by the police. So we set out to the scene. What we saw there was horrible. I was 50 years old at the time but I'm still suffering the consequences of what I saw to this day. It might be a vulgar expression, but we were in blood up to our knees. People were moaning, asking for help, crying out for help. We tried to assist as best we could. First we collected the most seriously injured, then the ones who were less seriously injured, and we sent them all to hospital in Djakovica. They were admitted to hospital there and the most seriously injured were transferred to Pristina or perhaps to hospitals in Serbia, in the interior of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to the victims in this instance what was the ethnicity of the same?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: These people were Albanians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if you go very briefly to page 30, line 5, and then the answer at line 9, can I take it that's something different?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Different from the one we're discussing now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Although that question is identical, but can we clarify who the attackers were in the incident at line 13 -- line 9 of page 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zlatkovic, with respect to the attack on the refugee settlement at Maja -- Maja, M-a-j-a I believe it is, where the 50 or so people -- where the 50 or so people were situated, what -- when you say they were attacked at night and quite a few people were killed and injured at lines 15 and 16, including Darko Ulatovic, who was a retarded young man, could you tell us who was responsible for this attack?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: I think NATO was responsible for that attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just for the sake of clarity, this incident occurred -- this incident is a different incident than the one we were discussing on the road wherein the -- wherein near the Bistrazin bridge there were ethnic Albanian victims; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we could focus back again on the incident near the Bistrazin bridge wherein the convoy was struck by NATO. I think we have a recording from the crime scene, recording at 6D295, and if we -- I don't want to show the entire tape although we might at some point in time tender it into evidence from the bar table. It's only about 20 minutes long but I don't think we need to see the whole thing. I have some segments set up, if we could play the first segment, and if you could describe for us if this is the -- if this comports with your recollection of the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was that the scene of the column of civilians that was struck on the roadway near the Bistrazin bridge by NATO forces?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: From Maja, this is from Maja.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we look at the next segment I believe it -- well, let's -- you indicated some of these people had been sent -- one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before we move, we've got two references to Maja.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's a distinction that I guess is not coming through on the translation. The one we're looking at is Meja, M-e-j-a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's what I thought, and that is the second of the two incidents?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can look at the next -- the next segment from the videotape, you indicated that certain people had been transported by the help that arrived to the hospital in Djakovica of these ethnic Albanians. If we could play this next portion of the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Does this comport with your recollection of the -- some of the persons that were evacuated and does the date -- more importantly, does the date at the bottom left coincide with your recollections of the attack on the roadway outside Meja by NATO forces?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: The time and the date, yes, and this is the hospital in Djakovica, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And could you tell us what the safety circumstances were like for conducting that investigation?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Very poor, very poor. All of us were in danger. When the planes flew over, some of my colleagues were so frightened that they began to vomit and flee towards a valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you indicated that the efforts to assist the people -- I have another short -- short video segment, 6D1633, which is some -- another tape, not the crime scene tape, bought rather a tape from a -- first of all, were there media journalists present at the site following the attack, regarding the efforts to ...

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, the media were there. I don't know who informed them, but while we were doing our job they turned up. It was towards the end of our work when they arrived, and they filmed the whole event. I can tell you that I hadn't been home for two months, my family didn't know what had happened to me. In the evening they saw me on television helping some people, and when I returned to Vranje people came up to me to congratulate me on what I had done.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You indicated that your family didn't know what had happened to you. What were the abilities to communicate with the rest of Serbia like in Djakovica during this time-period, the middle of April 1999?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: We couldn't call home because there were no mobile phones and no regular lines. Only those who had satellite telephones could perhaps use those, but among the Serbs there weren't any.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now if we could play the clip 6D1633, and if I could ask you while the clip is playing to tell us if you can identify any of the persons or scenes depicted and give us further information about the same. Again, this clip is short, it should be only about a minute long.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop, stop. I recognise policeman Dragan Stojanovic here, his family lived in the village of Dubrava, near Glodjane. The terrorists beat up his brother. This Dragan Stojanovic was a policeman in the police station in Djakovica, and here he's carrying a child in his arms and the mother of the child is carrying another one and another one is following them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Are these -- are these his family or are these other persons?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. Dragan Stojanovic is a Serb, he's a policeman, he worked in Djakovica. His family until the 24th of March, 1998, lived in the village of Dubrava near Glodjane but they were constantly mistreated.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay, we're talking about this specific video footage here. Who is he carrying?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: He's carrying an Albanian child.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was he one of the officers who was on the scene to offer assistance to the victims of this NATO attack?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we can play the clip further.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Here we see -- can you go back a bit. We also engaged the public utility company so that the corpses of those who had been killed could be taken to the morgue in Djakovica hospital and identified there. Here we see the employees of the public utility company attempting to load these dead people onto vehicles.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Here I recognise myself, I'm in the last part, together with an employee of the utility company and another person. We are helping a wounded woman, helping to get her to the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we could just play the clip all the way through, I think there's only a little bit left.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. That's that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, just very briefly. I note that no transcript has been provided for this video or the previous -- I don't mean to interrupt my colleague during his examination, but we have no transcript. So if he intends to rely on what is being said in this video and the previous one, we would appreciate receiving a transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the position, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that the pictures speak for themselves and the commentary of Mr. Zlatkovic based upon his personal experience is all that I'm relying upon. I'm not relying on the -- the news account or overlay on the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Now we have clarification of the date of the second of these two events. Can you clarify the position in relation to the first one?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zlatkovic, do you recall the first incident we talked about, the attack on the refugee centre at Maja, where the refugees from Croatia were situated, do you know when approximately that occurred in relation to this event perhaps or any date that you can provide us with?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: I remember it was in April, both events were in April, I think -- well, I can't give you the precise date. I don't recall. But it was around the 20th, 20 something.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And -- all right. We have that. Now if I could turn to 6D536 for a moment, I believe this is another incident on one of the roadways, the communication Djakovica-Dolac towards the village of Crmljanje, this is a document that hopefully will be getting up soon. If you could take a moment to review this document, sir, and maybe to assist with this kind of lengthy -- I can provide a hard copy to the witness so as to speed things up and alleviate the need to have all the pages on e-court for his review. This is 6D536. Do you -- do you recall this -- this incident and do you recall the circumstances of the same and could you give us any additional information with regard to this particular incident and this -- who is responsible for this attack, for instance?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Concerning this incident, it was my colleague Radovan Nikolic who dealt with this. I was not tasked with this case, so I'm not familiar with what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Let's move along to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that document will not be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can move along to your statement beginning at paragraph 39 onwards talks about on-site investigations following a meeting at the end of April 1999. Do you recall how long after this meeting with the chief of the OKP of the SUP Djakovica were the investigative teams able to actually go out to the scene in Reka Kec to perform their investigative work?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At paragraph 39 of your statement you describe being informed of the suspected existence of some bodies in the valley known as the Reka Kec, and then you talk about when conditions were made possible. You -- the teams were sent out into the field. Do you recall approximately how long after finding the initial information were the investigators able to go out onto the scene to perform their on-site investigations in the area known as Reka Kec?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: After the information was received by the head of the criminal police department in the area of Reka Kec, or Caragoj as they refer to it, we learned of certain corpses and tried to set out the same day to carry out an on-site investigation. We were unable to reach Mrekovci [phoen] because there were NATO air-strikes next to the border. These villages are some 30 kilometres from Djakovica next to the border. We tried several days to go there, and I think it took five or six days from the moment when we were notified that there were corpses there to the point at which we finally visited a location, I mean my team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can ask a general question first. In your statement you describe at paragraph 42 how some of the bodies that you processed or investigated were wearing uniforms. Could you give us more details about that.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: I can tell you this: I told you that we had several attempts to reach those locations. Finally, on the fifth or the sixth day we managed to go there. In addition to the air-strikes there were also terrorists who were active in the area. When we arrived at the scene we found I think between 20 and 25 of them in the area where I was with my team, between 20 and 25. The bodies were mainly male. The age was between 20 and 30. They had individual pieces of uniform on them, either black overalls or parts of camouflage uniforms. On certain individuals we found say camouflage shorts and black pants as well as boots. In any case, they had different clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect to these bodies that your teams uncovered could you describe for us what kind of positions these bodies were discovered in. Are we talking about -- in terms of groupings. Were there large groupings, small groupings, individual bodies? How would you describe the specific bodies that were uncovered or recovered or processed as part of these investigations up into the Reka Kec region?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: The bodies were found in different locations. Some of them were in attics of the houses there, others were in stables, then behind walls, some of the bodies were in the nearby woods. And for the most part we would find individual bodies or pairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the -- sir, if you could repeat what you said about the -- the part that you weren't sure whether it could be translated into English because unfortunately it's not in the transcript and unfortunately it's a word that I'm familiar with in Serbian so I can't assist in terms of completing your testimony in that regard. Where the bodies were found you said that they were found and you mentioned a word and you said you were not sure how that translates into English. Could you please repeat where in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: I will repeat. Those were stables for cattle, we call them "pljevnje," or rather, that's where the feed is supposed to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And we heard some allegations -- first of all, are you familiar with a joint check-point outside of Meja and did you have to go by that check-point in order to get to the sites that you investigated as part of in on-site investigation?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: I did pass through.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We've heard some allegations here about bodies by that check-point. Did you have occasion to witness any bodies or any investigative teams working on bodies at that check-point whatsoever during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: I conducted on-site investigations in Ramoc, Popovac, Korenica, and towards Ponosevac. At the place where the check-point was, when I passed by, or rather, while I was there, I passed by on at least three or four occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you describe for us a little bit the procedures that were followed with regard to these investigations in documenting the corpses that were found or recovered.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: When a body of a killed soldier would be found or crime scene technicians, usually it took finger-prints. We used the so-called dactyloscopic test so as to be able to compare that with the file that we may have or identification papers in case those people had ever had an ID issued anywhere in Yugoslavia. That is how we went about identifying them. We also paid attention to any tattoos that would be described, as well as items of clothing, footwear, and anything that could help us in further identification of those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And approximately how many teams were out in the field simultaneously with respect to the various sites that were investigated?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all the Djakovica SUP was short of staff. We were unable to have five or six teams so as to be able to do the whole work in a day. We had three teams at the most, we would dispatch them. We never sent out large groups in the field because they could get hurt either by NATO air-strikes or minefields planted by terrorists. We didn't want to have people being wounded or killed. Usually we would have one, two, or three teams; however, this took several days, over ten days I'd say.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You left, I believe, on May the 15th from Djakovica and were reassigned back to the -- back to Vranje where you are from. Was the overall investigation completed by the time you had left the SUP Djakovica on the 15th of May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: Sometime in April I was wounded during a NATO air-strike in Ljubunar. I wasn't hit by a piece of shrapnel, but rather I simply sprained my ankle. I was injured. So for about 15 to 20 days I was hors de combat. Around the 15th of April [as interpreted] I was allowed to return home since I no longer felt I was of assistance to those there. I asked to be sent back, it was approved, and on the 15th of May, 1999, I returned to Vranje. We collected all the information in one place, we left it at the SUP. We didn't know what to expect and we didn't want to have the information dispersed. In any case, I don't know whether the overall investigation was completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just to clarify things, there's two dates -- it's the 15th of May that you returned to Vranje, is that correct? There's two dates showing up in your answer and I think the 15th of May is mentioned in paragraph 43 of your statement. You returned to Vranje the 15th of May; is that correct? You have to answer out loud, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: 15 to 20 days before I left. I asked to be sent back because I was injured and they met my request. On the 15th of May I left the Djakovica SUP via Prizren, Sar-Planina, and Brezovica as well as Urosevac, finally to reach Vranje.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in the course of the investigation, at least for the time-period that you were there performing the investigation, how many bodies had been recovered, documented, and investigated in total, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ZLATKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as my team goes, I know that there were between 20 and 25. As for the others, I don't know. I don't know what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I've completed all the direct examination that I had foreseen for this witness, including the matters that I had prepared this morning that were excess from the -- that didn't make it into the written statement. So I thank Your Honours for the opportunity to prepare for this witness and I pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Zlatkovic, is this an incident about which you got no explanation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid I didn't understand. Would you please repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You became involved in this investigation at the end of April and you were involved for some time. Now, during the time you were involved was there any explanation for how these bodies came to be there that came to light?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how it was learned that the bodies were there. The several teams including mine were told by the chief of the SUP that there were bodies in the valley. As for how they were killed, I truly don't know. I'm not an expert in that field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, but you've been able to tell us how many other bodies were killed because you were involved in the investigation, you can tell us about snipers shooting people in the back of the head and you can tell us about ambushes and so on as the result of the on-site investigation. Now, were you not able to piece together any explanation of the cause of death of these bodies or the circumstances in which they came to be killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid there was a misunderstanding. The people were killed by bullets; however, I don't know whether they were killed in combat or in some other way. The investigation was supposed to be completed; however, at a certain point I left and I don't know what was then done subsequently. I think ballistic expertise was supposed to take place and additional checks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but just being a bit more basic than that, the evidence you've given suggests that some of them may have been combatants. But if they were killed in combat you would expect that whoever was involved would have arranged for the battle-field to be cleared up or disclosed that there was a need for that to be done. Is that not the situation that you would normally expect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the term of clearing up terrain, I'm not certain what it actually means since it doesn't exist in the police. It is most likely that they were killed in combat and I conclude that based on the positions at which they were, these were elevations, locations from which one could open fire. We collected spent cartridges, projectiles, parts of hand-grenades, all that was collected in order to try and shed light on the crime, or rather, the incident which had taken place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But do I rightly understand, though, that as far as you're concerned, with whom they might have been engaged in combat remains a mystery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right, Your Honour, I still don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You don't find that strange if it was a genuine combat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is most likely that two sides clashed, I mean the terrorists side and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the other side was the police, army, as one would expect in a time of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if it was the police, would you not know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm a crime inspector, it is separate in terms of administration at the level of the republican SUP. In the SUP itself we are talking about two separate administrations. Within the SUP we have the criminal police department and then there is the uniformed police department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So in your system the criminal investigators, such as yourself, would be sent out to investigate deaths that may have been in combat without being told one way or another whether the police had been involved in combat in that area because they were in a different police department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were not told that. We carried out on-site investigations in order to collect information and to gather facts in order to arrive at a conclusion subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Bakrac, you will have cross-examination, will you?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as I have already asked you, I wish to cross-examine tomorrow, if I may. If there is going to be any, it shouldn't last more than five to ten minutes; therefore, I won't need much time tomorrow, it will take only a minimum of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I understand that. But you don't know at the moment whether you will have any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it could happen that I won't have any. If there will be any, that will depend on the documents which I will review, and in any case it will be short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I take it, Ms. Kravetz, your position remains the same as it was?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that I will proceed tomorrow and I will also be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zlatkovic, connected with the procedural difficulties we were discussing this morning, it's not possible to proceed further at this stage with the hearing of your evidence, it will have to continue tomorrow; that will be at 9.00 tomorrow morning, it will be in this courtroom. So you need to be back here ready to continue at 9.00. Meanwhile, it is an important rule that you must have no communication with anyone at all about any aspect of the evidence in this case. You can talk to whoever you like about whatever you like as long as you have no communication about the evidence in the case. Now could you please leave the courtroom with the usher and we will see you again tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 15th day of April, 2008, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.56 p.m.,
